bibliography.note: Bry, C., Basset, E., Rognon, X. & Bonamy, F. 1992. Analysis of sibling cannibalism among pike, Esox lucius, juveniles reared under semi-natural conditions. Environmental Biology of Fishes 35(1): 75–84, doi:10.1007/BF00001160. The entry agrees.

claims.claim: in ponds, cannibals were 7.8 % of ~100-mm juveniles at low density but 41.3 % at high density (Bry et al. 1992, abstract)
claims.note: Abstract only (not usable to confirm). It says that 'At a mean total length of 100 mm' and initial stocking of 6 and 18 larvae m⁻² (12 and 36 larvae m⁻³) in outdoor rearing ponds, 'the average proportions of cannibals in the populations of juveniles were 7.8% and 41.3%', and that the cannibals made up 15.5 % and 65.9 % of total pike biomass. Matches the paper.

claims.claim: the share of pond juveniles that became cannibals rose from 7.8 % to 41.3 % as larval density tripled (Bry et al. 1992; abstract only)
claims.note: Abstract only. 6 → 18 larvae m⁻² is a tripling, so the wording matches the abstract; the shares are at a mean total length of 100 mm, which the §3.7.7 sentence omits.

notes: OpenAlex knows no free copy. Useful abstract values beyond the paper's: no cannibalism during the larval period (13–35 mm TL), only in juveniles; at 18 larvae m⁻² cannibalism began 21 days after first feeding (mean TL 60 mm); prey were swallowed whole, head first; 'The overall mean ratio of pike prey length to pike cannibal length was 66.2%', and prey head depth averaged 87.6 % of the cannibal's mouth width. The 66 % mean prey:cannibal length ratio in juvenile pike is larger than the 0.03–0.55 range §3.7.7 takes from Persson, Bertolo & De Roos 2006 for Swedish lake pike and bears on the project's '20-cm pickerel at risk only from pickerel of 36–40 cm or more' estimate (a 0.66 ratio would put a 20-cm pickerel at risk from a ~30-cm one) — worth a look when the full text is read.
